name: Water

description.intuition: Water is the liquid that covers most of Earth and is needed by every living thing.
description.science: Each water molecule has one oxygen atom bonded to two hydrogen atoms. The bent shape and polar bonds make water an excellent solvent for ionic substances.
description.technical: Density 0.997 g/cm³ at 25 °C (maximum 1.000 g/cm³ near 4 °C). Specific heat about 4.18 J/(g·K). Pure water conducts electricity poorly; dissolved ions make it conductive.

sources: CRC Handbook of Chemistry and Physics (typical tabulated values)
NIST Chemistry WebBook (webbook.nist.gov)

name: Ice (solid water)

description.intuition: Ice is frozen water, and it floats because it is less dense than liquid water.
description.science: In ice, hydrogen bonds hold water molecules in an open hexagonal lattice, which takes up more space than the liquid.
description.technical: Density about 0.917 g/cm³ at 0 °C; melting requires 334 J/g (latent heat of fusion). Same substance as water, different physical state.

sources: CRC Handbook of Chemistry and Physics (typical tabulated values)
notes: Ice and water are one substance (H2O) in two states; the database keeps a separate entry only so the solid's density and heat capacity can be shown.

name: Carbon dioxide

description.intuition: Carbon dioxide is the gas you breathe out and the bubbles in fizzy drinks.
description.science: A linear molecule with one carbon atom double-bonded to two oxygen atoms. It dissolves slightly in water, forming a weakly acidic solution.
description.technical: Sublimes at −78.5 °C (194.7 K) at 1 atm; it has no liquid phase below 5.1 atm. Molar mass 44.01 g/mol, so it is denser than air.

sources: CRC Handbook of Chemistry and Physics (typical tabulated values)
NIST Chemistry WebBook (webbook.nist.gov)
notes: boilingPointK holds the sublimation point at 1 atm. Solubility about 0.033 mol/L at 25 °C under 1 atm of pure CO2.

name: Oxygen

description.intuition: Oxygen is the part of the air that we, and fires, need.
description.science: O₂ molecules make up about 21 % of air. Oxygen is highly electronegative and takes part in combustion and corrosion.
description.technical: Boils at 90.19 K. Supports combustion: materials burn much more vigorously in pure oxygen than in air.

sources: CRC Handbook of Chemistry and Physics (typical tabulated values)
NIST Chemistry WebBook (webbook.nist.gov)
notes: Solubility in water at 25 °C under 1 atm of the pure gas.

name: Hydrogen

description.intuition: Hydrogen is the lightest gas.
description.science: H₂ molecules are made of two hydrogen atoms sharing a pair of electrons. Hydrogen burns with oxygen to form water, releasing a lot of energy.
description.technical: Boils at 20.27 K. Flammable over a very wide range of concentrations in air, which is why real hydrogen handling requires strict safety controls.

sources: CRC Handbook of Chemistry and Physics (typical tabulated values)
NIST Chemistry WebBook (webbook.nist.gov)
notes: Solubility in water at 25 °C under 1 atm of the pure gas.

name: Nitrogen

description.intuition: Nitrogen is the main gas in air.
description.science: N₂ molecules are held together by a strong triple bond, which makes nitrogen unreactive under ordinary conditions.
description.technical: About 78 % of dry air by volume. Boils at 77.36 K.

sources: CRC Handbook of Chemistry and Physics (typical tabulated values)
NIST Chemistry WebBook (webbook.nist.gov)
notes: Solubility in water at 25 °C under 1 atm of the pure gas.

name: Chlorine

description.intuition: Chlorine is a pale green-yellow gas used to make water safe to drink.
description.science: Cl₂ is a reactive halogen and a strong oxidising agent. It is produced industrially by electrolysis of brine (the chlor-alkali process).
description.technical: Boils at 239.1 K. Toxic: in this game it only appears as a sealed product of brine electrolysis that can be converted to hydrochloric acid.

hazard: Toxic gas in reality. The game never uses it outside a sealed apparatus.
sources: CRC Handbook of Chemistry and Physics (typical tabulated values)
notes: Solubility in water at 25 °C under 1 atm of the pure gas.

name: Hydrogen chloride (hydrochloric acid when dissolved)

description.intuition: Dissolved in water, hydrogen chloride forms hydrochloric acid, a strong acid also found in your stomach.
description.science: HCl ionises completely in water into H⁺ (as H₃O⁺) and Cl⁻ ions, so it is a strong acid.
description.technical: In the game, acid reagents are dilute (1 mol/L). Concentrated hydrochloric acid is corrosive and gives off choking fumes.

hazard: Corrosive. The game uses only dilute solutions.
sources: CRC Handbook of Chemistry and Physics (typical tabulated values)
notes: Very soluble in water (about 720 g/L at 20 °C); in the game it stays dissolved whenever liquid water is present.

name: Sodium chloride (salt)

description.intuition: Table salt. It dissolves in water and gives seawater its taste.
description.science: An ionic compound: a lattice of Na⁺ and Cl⁻ ions held together by electrostatic attraction. Dissolving salt is a physical change; the ions separate but no new substance forms.
description.technical: Melts at 801 °C. Solubility about 360 g per litre of water at 25 °C (≈6.1 mol/L). Crystals are cubic.

sources: CRC Handbook of Chemistry and Physics (typical tabulated values)

name: Iron

description.intuition: Iron is a strong, magnetic metal used to make steel.
description.science: A transition metal; its atoms are held together by metallic bonding (a lattice of ions in a 'sea' of shared electrons), which makes it conduct electricity and heat.
description.technical: Density 7.874 g/cm³; melts at 1538 °C. Ferromagnetic below 770 °C (the Curie temperature). Real ingots usually contain small amounts of carbon and other elements.

sources: CRC Handbook of Chemistry and Physics (typical tabulated values)

name: Copper

description.intuition: Copper is the reddish metal used in electrical wires.
description.science: Metallic bonding with one loosely held outer electron per atom gives copper very high electrical conductivity.
description.technical: Density 8.96 g/cm³, resistivity 1.68×10⁻⁸ Ω·m at 20 °C, thermal conductivity about 400 W/(m·K).

sources: CRC Handbook of Chemistry and Physics (typical tabulated values)

name: Gold

description.intuition: Gold is a heavy, shiny metal that never rusts.
description.science: Gold is very unreactive (a 'noble' metal), so it is found uncombined in nature.
description.technical: Density 19.3 g/cm³ — much denser than iron or lead — which is why density testing can reveal fake gold.

sources: CRC Handbook of Chemistry and Physics (typical tabulated values)

name: Silicon dioxide (silica, quartz)

description.intuition: Silica is what most sand and quartz crystals are made of.
description.science: A giant covalent network: every silicon atom is bonded to four oxygen atoms and every oxygen to two silicon atoms. This makes quartz hard and gives it a high melting point.
description.technical: Density 2.65 g/cm³ for quartz. Glass is made mainly from silica, usually with sodium and calcium oxides added to lower the melting temperature.

sources: CRC Handbook of Chemistry and Physics (typical tabulated values)
notes: Melting point given for quartz/cristobalite (~1713 °C); boiling point is approximate.

name: Calcium carbonate (calcite)

description.intuition: Calcium carbonate is limestone, chalk, calcite and seashells.
description.science: An ionic compound of Ca²⁺ and carbonate (CO₃²⁻) ions. It reacts with acids to release carbon dioxide and decomposes into lime when strongly heated.
description.technical: Density 2.71 g/cm³ (calcite). Practically insoluble in pure water (≈0.013 g/L). Decomposes above about 825 °C rather than melting at atmospheric pressure.

sources: CRC Handbook of Chemistry and Physics (typical tabulated values)

name: Calcium oxide (quicklime)

description.intuition: Quicklime is made by baking limestone and is used to make cement and mortar.
description.science: An ionic oxide that reacts with water to form calcium hydroxide, releasing a lot of heat.
description.technical: Melts at about 2613 °C. Reacts exothermically with water (slaking).

sources: CRC Handbook of Chemistry and Physics (typical tabulated values)

name: Calcium hydroxide (slaked lime)

description.intuition: Slaked lime dissolves a little in water to make limewater, which turns milky with carbon dioxide.
description.science: A strong base with low solubility: the dissolved part is fully ionised into Ca²⁺ and OH⁻ ions.
description.technical: Solubility about 1.7 g/L at 20 °C (≈0.023 mol/L); a saturated solution has a pH of about 12.4. Decomposes to CaO above about 580 °C.

sources: CRC Handbook of Chemistry and Physics (typical tabulated values)

name: Calcium chloride

description.intuition: Calcium chloride is a salt used to melt ice on roads.
description.science: An ionic compound that dissolves readily in water to give Ca²⁺ and Cl⁻ ions; its solution is neutral.
description.technical: Dissolving anhydrous CaCl₂ releases heat. Very soluble (about 745 g/L at 20 °C).

sources: CRC Handbook of Chemistry and Physics (typical tabulated values)

name: Sodium hydroxide

description.intuition: Sodium hydroxide is a strong base used to make soap.
description.science: It dissociates completely in water into Na⁺ and OH⁻ ions, so even dilute solutions are strongly basic.
description.technical: The game uses only dilute (1 mol/L) solutions. Concentrated sodium hydroxide is highly corrosive to skin and eyes.

hazard: Corrosive. The game uses only dilute solutions.
sources: CRC Handbook of Chemistry and Physics (typical tabulated values)

name: Acetic acid (in vinegar)

description.intuition: Acetic acid gives vinegar its sour taste and smell.
description.science: A weak acid: in water only a small fraction of molecules give up an H⁺ ion (pKa = 4.76 at 25 °C).
description.technical: Household vinegar is roughly 5 % acetic acid by mass (≈0.8 mol/L), with a pH near 2.4–2.5.

sources: CRC Handbook of Chemistry and Physics (typical tabulated values)

name: Sodium acetate

description.intuition: Sodium acetate is the salt formed when vinegar is neutralised by sodium hydroxide; it is used in reusable hand warmers.
description.science: It contains acetate, the conjugate base of acetic acid, so its solution is slightly basic.
description.technical: A 0.1 mol/L solution has a pH of about 8.9.

sources: CRC Handbook of Chemistry and Physics (typical tabulated values)

name: Calcium acetate

description.intuition: Calcium acetate forms when vinegar dissolves limestone or eggshells.
description.science: An ionic salt of Ca²⁺ and acetate ions; acetate is a weak base.
description.technical: Decomposes on strong heating rather than melting. Density approximate.

sources: CRC Handbook of Chemistry and Physics (typical tabulated values)

name: Iron(III) oxide (hematite)

description.intuition: Iron(III) oxide is the red-brown material in rust and in many iron ores.
description.science: Each formula unit contains two Fe³⁺ ions and three O²⁻ ions. Carbon or carbon monoxide can remove the oxygen to produce iron metal (reduction).
description.technical: Density about 5.25 g/cm³ (hematite). Melts at about 1565 °C.

sources: CRC Handbook of Chemistry and Physics (typical tabulated values)

name: Iron(II,III) oxide (magnetite)

description.intuition: Magnetite is a black, naturally magnetic iron ore.
description.science: It contains both Fe²⁺ and Fe³⁺ ions; it is the most magnetic naturally occurring mineral.
description.technical: Density about 5.17 g/cm³. Lodestones are naturally magnetised magnetite.

sources: CRC Handbook of Chemistry and Physics (typical tabulated values)

name: Copper(II) oxide

description.intuition: Copper(II) oxide is the black coating that forms when copper is heated in air.
description.science: Copper atoms lose two electrons to oxygen, forming Cu²⁺ and O²⁻ ions. Heated copper gains mass as it combines with oxygen from the air.
description.technical: Density about 6.3 g/cm³; decomposes near 1326 °C.

sources: CRC Handbook of Chemistry and Physics (typical tabulated values)

name: Carbon (graphite)

description.intuition: Graphite is the soft, grey form of carbon in pencils.
description.science: Carbon atoms form flat sheets of hexagons. Electrons can move along the sheets, so graphite conducts electricity, while weak forces between sheets make it slippery.
description.technical: Sublimes at about 3900 K at atmospheric pressure. Density 2.09–2.26 g/cm³ depending on form.

sources: CRC Handbook of Chemistry and Physics (typical tabulated values)

name: Carbon (diamond)

description.intuition: Diamond is the hardest natural material, made only of carbon.
description.science: Each carbon atom is bonded to four others in a rigid 3-D network. There are no free electrons, so diamond is an electrical insulator, but it conducts heat extremely well.
description.technical: Density 3.51 g/cm³. Diamond and graphite are allotropes: the same element with different structures.

sources: CRC Handbook of Chemistry and Physics (typical tabulated values)

name: Carbon monoxide

description.intuition: Carbon monoxide is an invisible gas formed when fuel burns with too little oxygen.
description.science: In a blast furnace, carbon monoxide removes oxygen from iron ore (it acts as a reducing agent).
description.technical: Toxic because it binds to haemoglobin much more strongly than oxygen. In the game it is only an intermediate inside smelting equipment.

sources: CRC Handbook of Chemistry and Physics (typical tabulated values)
notes: Solubility in water at 25 °C under 1 atm of the pure gas.

name: Chalcopyrite

description.intuition: Chalcopyrite is a brassy-yellow mineral and the most important copper ore.
description.science: A copper iron sulfide. Copper is extracted by roasting and smelting, which also removes the sulfur.
description.technical: Density 4.1–4.3 g/cm³; Mohs hardness 3.5–4. Melting value approximate.

sources: CRC Handbook of Chemistry and Physics (typical tabulated values)

name: Sucrose (table sugar)

description.intuition: Sucrose is ordinary table sugar.
description.science: A molecular compound made of glucose and fructose units. Dissolving sugar is a physical change; the solution does not conduct because no ions form.
description.technical: Decomposes (caramelises) at about 186 °C instead of boiling. Very soluble in water.

sources: CRC Handbook of Chemistry and Physics (typical tabulated values)

name: Ethanol

description.intuition: Ethanol is the alcohol in drinks and a common laboratory solvent.
description.science: A small polar molecule that mixes with water in all proportions; it boils at a lower temperature than water, which is why distillation can separate the two.
description.technical: Boils at 78.4 °C. Flammable.

sources: CRC Handbook of Chemistry and Physics (typical tabulated values)

name: Sodium carbonate (washing soda)

description.intuition: Sodium carbonate is washing soda, used in glass-making.
description.science: Carbonate ions accept H⁺ from water, making the solution basic.
description.technical: A 0.1 mol/L solution has a pH of about 11.6.

sources: CRC Handbook of Chemistry and Physics (typical tabulated values)

name: Kaolinite (clay mineral)

description.intuition: Kaolinite is the main mineral in white clay and porcelain.
description.science: A layered aluminium silicate. Firing clay drives out water and transforms the minerals into hard ceramic.
description.technical: Density about 2.6 g/cm³. Clays are mixtures of several minerals; kaolinite is used here as a representative.

sources: CRC Handbook of Chemistry and Physics (typical tabulated values)

name: Beryl

description.intuition: Beryl is the mineral that emeralds and aquamarines are made of.
description.science: A ring silicate of beryllium and aluminium. Traces of chromium or vanadium make it green (emerald).
description.technical: Density 2.63–2.92 g/cm³; hardness 7.5–8.

sources: CRC Handbook of Chemistry and Physics (typical tabulated values)

name: Hydroxyapatite (bone mineral)

description.intuition: Hydroxyapatite is the hard mineral in bones and teeth.
description.science: A calcium phosphate mineral; in bone it is combined with the protein collagen.
description.technical: Density about 3.16 g/cm³. Real bone is a composite of mineral, protein and water.

sources: CRC Handbook of Chemistry and Physics (typical tabulated values)

name: Calcium sulfate (gypsum, anhydrous basis)

description.intuition: Calcium sulfate is the mineral in plaster and blackboard chalk (gypsum is its hydrated form).
description.science: An ionic compound of Ca²⁺ and sulfate ions; only slightly soluble in water.
description.technical: Anhydrite density 2.96 g/cm³; gypsum (CaSO₄·2H₂O) 2.32 g/cm³.

sources: CRC Handbook of Chemistry and Physics (typical tabulated values)

name: Sodium oxide

description.intuition: Sodium oxide is one of the ingredients that turns sand into ordinary glass.
description.science: A basic ionic oxide. In glass it breaks up the silica network, lowering the melting temperature; it reacts with water to form sodium hydroxide.
description.technical: Soda-lime glass is roughly 70–74 % SiO₂, 12–16 % Na₂O and 5–11 % CaO by mass.

sources: CRC Handbook of Chemistry and Physics (typical tabulated values)

name: Aluminium oxide (alumina)

description.intuition: Alumina is a very hard material; rubies and sapphires are crystals of it.
description.science: An ionic oxide with a very high lattice energy, which gives it a high melting point and hardness.
description.technical: Corundum density 3.95–4.1 g/cm³; Mohs hardness 9.

sources: CRC Handbook of Chemistry and Physics (typical tabulated values)

name: Iron(II) chloride

description.intuition: Iron(II) chloride forms a pale green solution when iron dissolves in hydrochloric acid.
description.science: Iron is more reactive than hydrogen, so it gives electrons to H⁺ ions: the iron is oxidised to Fe²⁺ and hydrogen gas is released.
description.technical: Fe²⁺ solutions slowly oxidise to Fe³⁺ in air (not modelled). Hydrolysis makes real solutions slightly acidic; the game treats the salt as neutral.

sources: CRC Handbook of Chemistry and Physics (typical tabulated values)
notes: Hydrolysis of Fe²⁺ is not modelled.

name: Iron(III) chloride

description.intuition: Iron(III) chloride gives a yellow-brown solution; it forms when acid dissolves rust.
description.science: The oxide ions in rust (Fe₂O₃) combine with H⁺ to form water, leaving Fe³⁺ and Cl⁻ ions in solution.
description.technical: Real FeCl₃ solutions are noticeably acidic because Fe³⁺ hydrolyses; the game treats the salt as neutral. Used industrially to etch copper circuit boards.

sources: CRC Handbook of Chemistry and Physics (typical tabulated values)
notes: Hydrolysis of Fe³⁺ is not modelled; anhydrous FeCl₃ sublimes/decomposes near 588 K.

name: Copper(II) chloride

description.intuition: Copper(II) chloride makes a blue-green solution.
description.science: Basic copper(II) oxide reacts with acid like any base: CuO + 2 H⁺ → Cu²⁺ + H₂O. The Cu²⁺ ions surrounded by water and chloride give the colour.
description.technical: Decomposes on strong heating. Copper compounds are harmful if swallowed.

sources: CRC Handbook of Chemistry and Physics (typical tabulated values)

name: Tricalcium silicate (alite)

description.intuition: Alite is the main ingredient of Portland cement; it is what makes concrete set hard.
description.science: Formed when limestone (CaO) and silica react in a kiln at about 1450 °C. With water it slowly forms calcium silicate hydrate, the 'glue' of concrete.
description.technical: Typically 50–70 % of Portland cement clinker. The hydration reactions are complex and not modelled.

sources: CRC Handbook of Chemistry and Physics (typical tabulated values)

name: Dicalcium silicate (belite)

description.intuition: Belite is the second cement mineral; it hardens more slowly than alite.
description.science: Forms at lower kiln temperatures than alite; contributes to long-term concrete strength.
description.technical: Typically 15–30 % of Portland cement clinker.

sources: CRC Handbook of Chemistry and Physics (typical tabulated values)
